name: Site enhancement oil (Synthol)

card.summary: Oil injected straight into muscle to make it look bigger; case reports document embolism, granulomas, nerve damage and infection.
card.note: Medical literature documents serious complications including pulmonary oil embolism and stroke; no clinical trials exist.

quick.overview:
Site enhancement oil (SEO), best known by the brand name Synthol, is an oily liquid injected into muscle to increase its apparent size or alter its shape. It has been associated mainly with bodybuilders who use it on lagging or disproportionate muscles, a practice called fluffing [1].

The injected oil does not build muscle tissue; it sits in the muscle as a deposit. Medical case reports describe a range of complications, and the wiki found no clinical trials of its use.
quick.mechanism: Wikipedia reports a Synthol formulation of about 85% oil, 7.5% lidocaine and 7.5% alcohol, with sesame oil commonly used; some people instead inject poly(methyl methacrylate) or paraffin oil [1]. The material distends the muscle mechanically. A Sunday Times report cited in Wikipedia says injected muscle is not truly developed and may droop under gravity [1].
quick.risks: Reported complications include pulmonary embolism, nerve damage, infection, sclerosing lipogranuloma, stroke, oil-filled granulomas, cysts and ulcers, and allergic vasculitis from sesame oil; a 2011 case study reported multi-organ dysfunction in a user of multiple substances [1]. Wikipedia says synthol is not restricted and is sold online, while PMMA for muscle shaping is prohibited in the US [1].

lead: Site enhancement oil (SEO), often called Synthol, santol or by the practice name "fluffing," is oil injected into muscle to increase its size or change its shape [1].

It is discussed as a hardmaxx or bodybuilding practice, mostly among competitive and professional bodybuilders who inject disproportionate or lagging muscles [1]. It adds volume without adding contractile muscle tissue.
The published record consists largely of case reports and short articles documenting complications. No clinical trials of site enhancement oil have been found.
infobox: Synthol not restricted and sold online; PMMA for muscle shaping prohibited in the US per Wikipedia [1]

paras: Wikipedia describes SEO as oil injected into muscle to enlarge it or change its shape. A cited paper from 2009 reports that Synthol is roughly 85% oil, 7.5% lidocaine and 7.5% alcohol [1]. Sesame oil has been identified in some mixtures, paraffin oil in Danish cases, and some practitioners inject poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) to shape rather than simply enlarge muscles [1].

According to Wikipedia, some bodybuilders, notably professionals, inject oil so muscles look more developed where they are lacking or disproportionate, and cited authors describe the practice as common among bodybuilders [1]. Wikipedia's sources date from 2000 onward, and it gives no detailed history.

Case reports and articles cited by Wikipedia list pulmonary embolism, nerve damage, infection, sclerosing lipogranuloma and stroke [1]. Oil-filled granulomas (oleomas), cysts and ulcers within muscle have been described in dermatology and Danish case reports, and sesame oil has triggered allergic vasculitis in one report [1]. A 2011 case study reported multi-organ dysfunction, possibly linked to prolonged hypercalcemia in a person using multiple substances [1]. Wikipedia says some cases may require surgery, a statement it flags as lacking a citation [1].
Wikipedia states that synthol is not restricted and many brands are sold online, while using PMMA to shape muscles is prohibited in the United States [1].
No studies found. The existing literature consists of case reports and short clinical notes describing complications in people who injected oils.

timeline.event: Earliest case report cited by Wikipedia, on oil-filled muscle granulomas [1].
ABC News and Sunday Times coverage of bodybuilders' oil injections [1].
Case study of multi-organ dysfunction in a multi-substance user [1].
